Issued at 209 AM CST Sun Nov 1 2026

/Near Term (Today and Tonight)/

Upper-air analysis depicts a split-flow regime over central 
Illinois early this morning, with a pair of compact shortwave 
troughs lifting across the Upper-Mississippi Valley and another 
translating across the Lower Ohio River Valley. Sufficient 
synoptic forcing--driven by both dCVA and gentle isentropic 
ascent--supports scattered showers into early afternoon. 
However, regional mesoscale soundings indicate persistent low- 
level dry air. Despite saturation in the 850-700mb layer, 
stubborn near- surface dryness will restrict coverage and 
intensity. While most locations receive between a trace and a 
few hundredths of an inch of precipitation, localized amounts up
to 0.25 inches are possible where low-level dry air is 
overcome, consistent with 00z REFS LPMM QPF. Abundant cloud 
cover will hold afternoon temperatures in the low- to mid-60s, 
keeping forecasts 3-5 degF cooler than NBM guidance.

Showery activity should taper off this evening as subsidence 
and weak ridging build in behind the departing shortwaves. 
Nevertheless, the period from overnight into Monday remains 
favorable for patchy, transient drizzle. This is primarily 
driven by warm, moist isentropic ascent lifting poleward across 
the Mid-Mississippi Valley Monday morning, augmented by an 
embedded shortwave rippling ahead of a deepening low pressure 
system over the Nebraska and South Dakota plains. Given the lack
of cloud ice nuclei, measurable rainfall will remain 
negligible. The greater impact could be on surface visibility, 
which could fall below 1 mile in spots if you believe REFS 
guidance. 

/Dynamic Midweek Storm System (Monday Night through Wednesday)/

Forecast uncertainty increases by Monday night as the jet 
stream buckles over the central U.S., driving multiple mid-level
shortwave troughs southward through midweek. Minor model 
discrepancies persist regarding trough phasing and precise 
frontal timing, though guidance consensus has converged on a 
Tuesday evening cold frontal passage across central Illinois.

As the synoptic low deepens and upper-level energy 
consolidates, the surface pressure gradient tightens 
significantly. EPS and GEFS mean wind gusts project peak speeds 
of 20-30 mph on Monday, increasing to 30-40 mph on Tuesday near 
the cold front. This dynamic system will draw mid-70s 
temperatures and a rich plume of Gulf moisture northward, 
pushing atmospheric precipitable water (PWAT) values near 1.75 
inches--approaching the 99th percentile for early November 
climatology. NBM Mean 48-hour QPF supports widespread rainfall 
totals around 1.0 inch through 6 AM Thursday (50-70% chance), 
with high-end 90th percentile forecasts indicating localized 
totals between 2.0 and 2.75 inches.

A few severe storms cannot be ruled out Tuesday evening. 
Kinematic fields will be robust, characterized by 40-50 kts of 
bulk shear. Although model-derived thermodynamics remain modest 
(MLCAPE < 150 J/kg), a narrow tongue of 60+ sfc dewpoints is 
forecast to surge ahead of the front. Sporadic damaging wind 
gusts present the main threat; however, low-level hodographs 
exhibit an elongated loop, suggesting a conditional tornado 
threat if sufficient low-level instability materializes to 
promote stretching.

/Late Week (Thursday through Next Weekend)/

Uncertainty remains regarding how the primary upper low evolves
late in the week. Ensemble guidance (GEFS and EPS) suggests the
low may meander over the Great Lakes through Thursday before 
departing Friday. Should this materialize, daily shower chances 
will persist through Thursday along the systems slow-moving 
deformation axis. Following an abbreviated break in 
precipitation on Friday, another frontal system approaches next 
weekend, bringing additional rain chances and potentially frosty
temperatures.
